explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Eve says, “With the help of the LORD I have brought forth a man…” (Genesis 4:1). She has just given birth to Cain, and the LORD is the One she names. I bet a lot of names could cross a new mom's mind right then, and she goes straight to Him.

The serpent did talk to Eve back in the garden (Genesis 3:1), so I see why it came to mind. But in this verse she gives the credit somewhere else. She says, “With the help of the LORD I have brought forth a man…” The serpent doesn't get a mention here.

Angels sound like a holy and helpful guess, friend, I'll give you that. But Eve doesn't say a word about angels in this verse. She says, “With the help of the LORD I have brought forth a man…” and that's the name she gives.
Yes, baker. Genesis 4:2 says Abel was a keeper of sheep. A shepherd works with a whole flock, and sheep never once ask for a raise. Hold on to that job, because it comes back later in this story.

A fisher on the sea? Somebody's got Abel out on a boat with a net, and I'm picturing the sheep waving from the shore. Genesis 4:2 says Abel was a keeper of sheep. His work is a flock, and that's the job that goes with his name.
Boat building is a big job, friend. I can barely build a cookie box without leaning on my mustache. Genesis 4:2 says Abel was a keeper of sheep, so his work is a flock, not a boat.

That's right. Genesis 4:2 says Cain was a tiller of the soil, so he works the ground. Abel has the sheep and Cain has the soil. Tilling is turning the ground over so something can grow. Me, I turn dough over and hope for cookies. Cain's work gets him a harvest.

Nets belong to someone who fishes, and no fishing happens in this passage. Genesis 4:2 says Cain was a tiller of the soil. So his tools are for the ground, not for the water. Soil is the word that fits.
Timber is a carpenter's word, baker. Cain's work is on the ground, not in a woodshop. Genesis 4:2 says he was a tiller of the soil. That's the word that goes in the blank.

explanations.answer: The best portions of the firstborn of his flock
explanations.explanation: That's the one. Genesis 4:4 says Abel brought the best portions of the firstborn of his flock. A shepherd brings from the sheep he keeps. It lines up with his job from verse 2.

explanations.answer: The first sheaves of grain from his field
explanations.explanation: Grain is a farmer's kind of gift, baker, so I see how the mix-up happens. But look at who brings what. Cain is the one who brought some of the fruit of the soil (Genesis 4:3). Abel, the shepherd, brought the best portions of the firstborn of his flock (Genesis 4:4). Don't hand Cain's basket to Abel!

explanations.answer: A pair of young doves from the hills
explanations.explanation: Doves are a nice thought, baker, but they aren't in this verse. Genesis 4:4 says Abel brought the best portions of the firstborn of his flock. His flock is where his offering comes from.

Not quite, baker. Genesis 4:4-5 says the LORD looked with favor on Abel and his offering, but He had no regard for Cain and his offering. So the two brothers are treated differently here. The text is plain about it.

Right. Genesis 4:4-5 says the LORD looked with favor on Abel and his offering, but He had no regard for Cain and his offering. Both brothers brought something, and the LORD responds differently. The text doesn't say why in these verses, so I won't guess.
Yes. Genesis 4:5 says Cain became very angry, and his countenance fell. That means his face dropped, friend. He doesn't hide it at all.
That would be one way to go about it, but the text doesn't say it happens. Genesis 4:5 says Cain became very angry, and his countenance fell. His reaction is anger, not a second offering.
A thank-you note would've been a classy move, baker. But Genesis 4:5 says Cain became very angry, and his countenance fell. Anger is what the text gives us.

That's right. The LORD says to Cain, “…sin is crouching at your door; it desires you, but you must master it.” (Genesis 4:7). Cain is already very angry by then (Genesis 4:5), and the LORD speaks to him before Cain kills Abel. Sin is the thing at the door, and the LORD says Cain must master it.
Crouching does sound like a big cat, friend. But the LORD doesn't say anything about a lion here. He says, “…sin is crouching at your door…” (Genesis 4:7).
Abel isn't the one crouching at the door, baker. The LORD says, “…sin is crouching at your door; it desires you, but you must master it.” (Genesis 4:7). Sin is the answer here.
Yes. The LORD says, “it desires you, but you must master it.” Sin wants something from Cain, and Cain is told to master it. The LORD tells him this up front.
Obey flips it around, baker. That would put sin in charge. The LORD says, “…you must master it.” (Genesis 4:7).
Welcome is what I say when a baker walks into my bakery, friend. It isn't what you say to something crouching at your door. The LORD says, “it desires you, but you must master it.” (Genesis 4:7).
That's right. Genesis 4:8 says Cain said to his brother Abel, “Let us go out to the field.” So Cain starts the invitation. The next part of that verse is a hard one.
The text says otherwise, baker. In Genesis 4:8, Cain says to his brother Abel, “Let us go out to the field.” So Cain is the one who asks Abel to go.
True. When the LORD asks, “Where is your brother Abel?” Cain answers, “I do not know!” (Genesis 4:9). He says it right to the LORD. It's a heavy moment, and the LORD keeps talking to him.
The text says otherwise, baker. Cain answers the LORD, “I do not know!” (Genesis 4:9). So he does answer, and that's what he says.
That's right. The LORD says, “The voice of your brother’s blood cries out to Me from the ground.” (Genesis 4:10). The LORD hears it, baker. That's a heavy line, and it's all in the text.

Abel's flock came up earlier, but it's not what cries out here. The LORD says, “The voice of your brother’s blood cries out to Me from the ground.” (Genesis 4:10). The word that goes in the blank is blood.
Offerings were all over the first part of this story, friend. But the LORD says, “The voice of your brother’s blood cries out to Me from the ground.” (Genesis 4:10). So the answer is blood.
Not this time, baker. The LORD tells Cain, “When you till the ground, it will no longer yield its produce to you.” (Genesis 4:12). For a farmer, that's a big change.

That's right. The LORD tells Cain, “When you till the ground, it will no longer yield its produce to you.” (Genesis 4:12). Cain's work was the soil, so this lands right on his job. It's part of what the LORD says to him.

Yes. The LORD tells Cain, “You will be a fugitive and a wanderer on the earth.” (Genesis 4:12). A man who farmed one patch of ground is told he'll be on the move. I think that sounds like a hard road.
That goes the opposite way, baker. The LORD says, “You will be a fugitive and a wanderer on the earth.” (Genesis 4:12). Cain is told he'll wander, not rule.
Cain's father doesn't come up in what the LORD says here. The LORD tells Cain, “You will be a fugitive and a wanderer on the earth.” (Genesis 4:12). That's the answer.

explanations.answer: Whoever finds him will kill him
explanations.explanation: That's what he says. Cain tells the LORD, “…whoever finds me will kill me.” (Genesis 4:14). He says it out loud. I think this one hurts to hear.

explanations.answer: The ground will swallow him up
explanations.explanation: The ground does come up in this passage, since it opened its mouth to receive Abel's blood (Genesis 4:11). But that's not what Cain says he's afraid of. He says, “…whoever finds me will kill me.” (Genesis 4:14).

explanations.answer: Wild beasts will hunt him down
explanations.explanation: Cain doesn't mention beasts, baker. He says, “…whoever finds me will kill me.” (Genesis 4:14). That's his fear in his own words.

That's right. Genesis 4:15 says, “And the LORD placed a mark on Cain, so that no one who found him would kill him.” The LORD answers Cain's fear with the mark. The text doesn't say what the mark looks like.
A crown would be quite a look, baker. But Genesis 4:15 says the LORD placed a mark on Cain, so that no one who found him would kill him. A crown isn't mentioned.
A robe is a nice thing to wear, friend, but it isn't in this verse. Genesis 4:15 says the LORD placed a mark on Cain, so that no one who found him would kill him. The word is mark.
Yes. Genesis 4:16 says Cain went out from the presence of the LORD and settled in the land of Nod, east of Eden. Nod is the name of the place. That's where his new life starts.

Goshen is a real place in Genesis, baker, but it shows up much later (Genesis 47:27). It's not where Cain settles. Genesis 4:16 says he went out from the presence of the LORD and settled in the land of Nod, east of Eden. Right book, different spot on the map, friend!
Moab shows up later in the Bible (Ruth 1:1). It's not where Cain goes. Genesis 4:16 says he settled in the land of Nod, east of Eden.
Yes. Genesis 4:17 says Cain built a city. Not a hut, not a shed, a whole city. I can barely keep my bakery counter clear of flour, so I'm impressed.
An altar is a fair guess, since offerings started this whole story. But Genesis 4:17 says Cain built a city. That's what he builds.
A tower does show up in Genesis later, with a city at Babel (Genesis 11:4). But Cain isn't building that one. Genesis 4:17 says he built a city.

That's right. Genesis 4:17 says Cain built a city and named it after his son Enoch. Enoch was born to Cain and his wife in that same verse. A whole city with the boy's name on it. I bet that boy never had to spell his name at a restaurant.

Adam is Cain's father, baker, and I get why his name jumped out first. He's the big name at the start of the chapter. But the city doesn't take his name. Genesis 4:17 says Cain named it after his son Enoch. If I named a whole city, I'd probably put a cookie stamper on the sign, and nobody would know where to park.

I think Abel's name hits hard in this chapter, friend, but it isn't the one on the city. Genesis 4:17 says Cain named it after his son Enoch. Abel is Cain's brother, not his son. The city carries the name of Cain's boy.

That's right. Lamech says, “If Cain is avenged sevenfold, then Lamech seventy-sevenfold.” (Genesis 4:24). He brings Cain up by name. Back in Genesis 4:15 the LORD said that if anyone slays Cain, Cain will be avenged sevenfold. Lamech goes from seven to seventy-seven, and I think that's quite a jump.
Abel isn't in Lamech's words, baker. Lamech says, “If Cain is avenged sevenfold, then Lamech seventy-sevenfold.” (Genesis 4:24). The name he uses is Cain.
Adam isn't who Lamech names. Lamech says, “If Cain is avenged sevenfold, then Lamech seventy-sevenfold.” (Genesis 4:24). Cain is the name that fits the blank.

Yes. Eve says, “God has granted me another seed in place of Abel, since Cain killed him.” (Genesis 4:25). She names Abel, and I think that means she hasn't forgotten him. The son she has just given birth to is Seth, and she says God granted him in place of Abel.
Cain is in the same verse, baker, but not in that spot. Eve says, “God has granted me another seed in place of Abel, since Cain killed him.” (Genesis 4:25). Abel is the answer.
Enoch is Cain's son, and he's in a different part of the story. Eve says, “God has granted me another seed in place of Abel, since Cain killed him.” (Genesis 4:25). So the name in the blank is Abel.
That's right. Genesis 4:26 says, “At that time men began to call upon the name of the LORD.” It comes right after Enosh, Seth's son, is born. The chapter ends on a good note, baker.

The text says otherwise, baker. Genesis 4:26 says, “At that time men began to call upon the name of the LORD.” That line comes right after Seth's son Enosh is born. So the statement is true, and men begin to call on the LORD's name at that time.
